For details on panel constraint modeling, refer 6 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. to the ResStock Technical Reference Guide (Reyna, et al., 2025). Duct sealing and insulation do not introduce new electrical loads or circuits, so they have no impact on the electrical panel. However, electrical panel metrics are included as a standard output for this and all other envelope measures. Any panel constraints appearing in the upgrade results reflect pre-existing conditions, as this measure does not worsen them. 4 Results This section first confirms the intended modeling approach for the upgrade by examining individual dwelling models, then shows the results if the upgrade were applied to the entire applicable building stock. 4.1 Single Building Example This section analyzes three example dwelling units that received duct sealing and insulation upgrades. Before the upgrades, each unit had uninsulated ducts with 20% leakage to the outside. After the upgrades, duct leakage was reduced to 5%, and R-8 insulation was added. The units are in Hawai‘i (climate zone 1A), North Carolina (climate zone 3A), and Alaska (climate zone 8AK), representing a range of climate conditions. The floor areas of these three dwelling units are different. Furthermore, the heating and cooling setpoint temperatures are also different. As a result, the baseline heating and cooling energy consumption can vary across the three example dwelling units, appearing either high or low. This section does not compare absolute energy consumption among these three example dwellings. Instead, it focuses solely on the percentage energy reduction achieved by the duct sealing and insulation. 4.1.1 Individual Building Annual Energy Consumption Figure 1 shows the annual energy consumption of three example dwelling units before and after duct sealing and insulation upgrades. The upgrades resulted in reductions across several heating- and cooling-related end uses, including heating, cooling, heating and cooling fans/pumps, heating heat pump backup, and associated backup fans/pumps. The example dwelling unit in Hawai‘i (climate zone 1A) uses electricity for both heating and cooling.
